beats.narration: An oral-history interview is not a transparent window into the past. It is a historical source created in a particular encounter. The narrator chooses what to remember and how to tell it; the interviewer shapes the path through questions and reactions; the recording medium and archive shape what later audiences can access. Begin with the source itself: who participated, when and where it was recorded, what language or languages were used, what the project asked about, and what permissions govern use.
beats.title: An Interview Is a Created Historical Source
beats.visualDirection: template:showcase-oral-history | A video interview frame sits beside date, location, participants, language, collection, and consent metadata.

beats.narration: A disciplined reading separates three layers. Testimony is what the narrator communicates. Context includes institutions, events, places, and social relationships that make the account legible. Interpretation is the argument a researcher builds by relating the interview to other evidence. Keeping these layers visible prevents an editor from presenting an inference as the narrator's own claim. It also preserves disagreement. Memory can be selective without being useless; the way an event is remembered may itself reveal identity, community, or later change.
beats.title: Separate Testimony, Context, and Interpretation
beats.visualDirection: template:showcase-oral-history | A table with columns labeled 'TESTIMONY', 'CONTEXT', and 'INTERPRETATION', illustrating how evidence stays distinct from a researcher's claim.

beats.narration: For Deaf oral histories, access is not a final technical add-on. Language, interpretation, captioning, transcription, camera framing, and interface design affect what can be expressed and what audiences receive. A transcript can support search and quotation, but it does not replace the embodied and linguistic information in a signed or spoken recording. Editors should document who translated or interpreted, preserve the original recording, and avoid forcing culturally specific expression into misleading written equivalents. Accessible presentation and historical accuracy are intertwined.
beats.title: Language and Access Shape Meaning
beats.visualDirection: template:showcase-oral-history | Connect narrator, interviewer, interpreter if present, transcriber, caption editor, archivist, and audience around the source.

beats.narration: Corroboration does not mean treating the narrator like a suspect. It means building a richer evidence field. Compare dates and names with club minutes, newspapers, photographs, directories, policy documents, and other interviews. When sources conflict, record the difference and ask what each source was positioned to know. A club record may document an official decision; an interview may reveal how that decision felt, who was excluded, or how community members adapted. Neither source automatically cancels the other.
beats.title: Corroborate Without Erasing Voice
beats.visualDirection: template:showcase-oral-history | Place interview memories on a timeline with club records, newspapers, photographs, and policy documents as parallel evidence tracks.

beats.narration: Before publishing, confirm that use matches the recorded permission and that names and sensitive material are handled as agreed. Provide accurate captions, a reviewed transcript, descriptive context, and provenance that identifies the collection and editorial choices. Do not simulate sign language or invent a narrator's voice. Make it easy for audiences to locate the original source and for participants or communities to raise corrections. Ethical oral history preserves agency while enabling study; accessibility is part of that preservation, not separate from it.
beats.title: Publish with Agency, Context, and Care
beats.visualDirection: template:showcase-oral-history | A publication checklist covers consent, naming, sensitive content, captions, transcript, description, provenance, and contact path.

claims.text: Oral-history practice requires preparation, informed participation, accurate descriptive information, careful preservation, and context that helps future audiences interpret the recorded interview.
